<!-- source: https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/blob/main/README.md -->

<p align="center">
  <img alt="kvz: native macOS Kubernetes. The control plane runs directly on macOS, one pod to Ready in 99 ms, Linux, macOS and native pods in one cluster." src="docs/assets/kvz-overview.png" width="100%">
</p>

# kvz

**Kubernetes that runs natively on your Mac.** kvz is a single binary, in the
spirit of k3s. The whole control plane (etcd, the API server, the scheduler and
the controllers) runs as one ordinary macOS process, with no Linux VM
underneath. Your pods run as:

- **Linux pods.** Each one is its own lightweight VM, ready in about 100 ms.
- **macOS pods.** A full macOS virtual machine you can `kubectl exec` into.
- **Native pods.** Plain macOS processes, for Xcode builds, code signing or
  anything that needs the real Mac.

You use it with the same `kubectl` and YAML you already know.

## Demo

<a href="https://youtu.be/GUZCElkfb1U">
  <img alt="Watch the kvz demo on YouTube" src="docs/assets/kvz-demo-video-v1.png" width="100%">
</a>

## Quick start

You need an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS 26 or later.

```sh
brew install kvz-platform/tap/kvz
kvz server                      # starts the cluster and prints how to connect
```

In a second terminal:

```sh
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kvz/kubeconfig.yaml
kubectl run web --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl get pods
```

That pod is a fresh Linux VM. The [getting started guide](docs/getting-started.md)
covers macOS and native pods, adding more Macs, running kvz in the background,
and building from source.

## How it compares

<p align="center">
  <img alt="kvz benchmark results against k3s in Lima and Apple container cluster" src="docs/assets/kvz-benchmarks.png" width="100%">
</p>

kvz is measured against **k3s in Lima** and **Apple's `container cluster`** on
three M4 Mac minis and a Mac Studio. It's faster on every lifecycle metric we
measured: startup, idle cost, API throughput, pod start, bursts and teardown.
It's slower at pod-to-pod bandwidth, because every pod is its own VM. No VM
pools, snapshots or pre-started pods are used to get these numbers.

Full tables and method: [docs/BENCHMARKS.md](docs/BENCHMARKS.md).

## Status

kvz is young. It passes all 454 tests of the Kubernetes certified-conformance
suite (Sonobuoy, Kubernetes v1.37.2, two nodes) and runs real workloads
(Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs, Services, Ingress, volumes, hostNetwork,
resource limits, HA control planes), but nobody has run it in production yet,
so please don't run production on it yet.

Found a security problem? Please report it privately, as described in
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). The brand assets (logos, banners, social images)
are in [docs/assets/brand-v1](docs/assets/brand-v1).

# Setting up a fleet of Macs

This guide turns several Macs (for example a shelf of Mac minis) into one kvz
cluster that starts on boot. It's written so that a person or an AI agent with
SSH access to the Macs can follow it step by step. Every step says how to check
that it worked before moving on.

If you only have one Mac, [Getting started](getting-started.md) is shorter.

## Contents

1. [Plan the cluster](#1-plan-the-cluster)
2. [Prepare every Mac](#2-prepare-every-mac)
3. [Network](#3-network)
4. [Install kvz on every Mac](#4-install-kvz-on-every-mac)
5. [Start the first server](#5-start-the-first-server)
6. [Add more servers (high availability only)](#6-add-more-servers-high-availability-only)
7. [Join the other Macs as agents](#7-join-the-other-macs-as-agents)
8. [Verify the cluster](#8-verify-the-cluster)
9. [Use the cluster from another computer](#9-use-the-cluster-from-another-computer)
10. [Day-2 operations](#10-day-2-operations)
11. [Troubleshooting](#11-troubleshooting)
12. [Getting help and reporting problems](#12-getting-help-and-reporting-problems)

## 1. Plan the cluster

Every Mac is either a **server** (runs the control plane: etcd, the API server,
the scheduler and controllers, plus a node) or an **agent** (only runs pods).

| Fleet size | Layout | Survives |
|---|---|---|
| 1 to 3 Macs | 1 server, the rest agents | nothing if the server Mac goes down (pods on agents keep running, but nothing can be changed) |
| 3 or more Macs, uptime matters | 3 servers with `--cluster-init`, the rest agents | the loss of any one server |

Use an odd number of servers (1, 3 or 5). Two servers are worse than one: etcd
needs a majority, so losing either of two stops the cluster.

Write down, before you start:

- each Mac's role, SSH address and host name;
- the address the Macs will use to reach each other (see [Network](#3-network));
- which Mac is the **first server**. Every other Mac joins through it.

## 2. Prepare every Mac

Do this on every Mac. All commands run over SSH as the user who will run kvz.
That user must be an administrator, and kvz runs in that user's login session.

### Requirements

```sh
uname -m                 # must print arm64 (Apple Silicon)
sw_vers -productVersion  # must be 26 or later
df -h ~                  # leave at least 20 GB free for images and volumes
```

### A unique name

kvz uses the host name, lowercased and without `.local`, as the node name, so
every Mac needs a different one. Two Macs called `Mac-mini` would fight over
the same node.

```sh
scutil --get LocalHostName
# if it isn't unique:
sudo scutil --set ComputerName  mini-01
sudo scutil --set HostName      mini-01
sudo scutil --set LocalHostName mini-01
```

You can also pass `--node-name` to kvz instead.

### Remote login, sleep and power

```sh
sudo systemsetup -setremotelogin on      # SSH (skip if you're already using it)
sudo pmset -a sleep 0 disksleep 0 displaysleep 0   # never sleep
sudo pmset -a autorestart 1              # power back on after a power cut
sudo pmset -a womp 1                     # wake for network access
```

Check with `pmset -g`: `sleep` must be `0`.

### Automatic login (required)

kvz runs as a launchd service in the user's **GUI login session**, because
Apple's Virtualization.framework, which every pod uses, needs one. A Mac that
reboots and sits at the login window runs no kvz. Turn on automatic login for
the kvz user:

- **System Settings → Users & Groups → Automatically log in as**, or
- over SSH: `sudo sysadminctl -autologin set -userName "$USER" -password '<that user’s password>'`

Automatic login is only possible with **FileVault turned off**
(`fdesetup status`). If FileVault must stay on, someone has to log in at the
console (or over Screen Sharing) after each reboot.

To check that a GUI session exists right now:

```sh
launchctl print gui/$(id -u) >/dev/null && echo "GUI session: yes"
```

## 3. Network

### Which address

Every Mac must reach every other Mac directly. kvz picks the address it
advertises (`--node-ip`) like this: a **Tailscale** address (100.64.0.0/10) if
the Mac has one, otherwise the first IPv4 address on an `en*` interface.

- **Tailscale (recommended for fleets).** Install it on every Mac and log in to
  the same tailnet. kvz uses the Tailscale addresses on its own, they don't
  change when the Macs move, and they avoid macOS's Local Network permission
  (see below). Make sure your tailnet ACL lets the Macs reach each other on the
  ports below.
- **A plain LAN.** Give each Mac a fixed address (a DHCP reservation). If a Mac
  has several interfaces (Wi-Fi and Ethernet, or a VPN), pass `--node-ip` with
  the address the others should use, to the server and to every agent.

### Ports

| Port | Protocol | Open on | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6443 | TCP | servers | Kubernetes API (`kubectl`, agents) |
| 6444 | TCP | servers | join endpoint (always the API port + 1) |
| 10250 | TCP | every Mac | API server to node: `kubectl logs`, `exec`, metrics |
| 6446 | TCP | every Mac | the pod network between Macs |
| 2380 | TCP | servers (HA only) | etcd between servers (mutual TLS) |
| 30000 to 32767 | TCP/UDP | every Mac | NodePort Services, if you use them |

### macOS firewall and Local Network permission

- If the macOS Application Firewall is on
  (`/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate`), allow
  kvz after installing it:

  ```sh
  sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --add "$(readlink -f "$(which kvz)")"
  sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --unblockapp "$(readlink -f "$(which kvz)")"
  ```

- macOS asks for **Local Network** permission the first time a program
  connects to another device on the LAN. On a headless Mac nobody sees that
  prompt, and the connections fail with `no route to host`. If an agent can't
  reach a server's LAN address even though `ping` works, open **System Settings
  → Privacy & Security → Local Network** (over Screen Sharing) and allow kvz,
  or use Tailscale addresses instead.

## 4. Install kvz on every Mac

```sh
brew install kvz-platform/tap/kvz
kvz version
```

Every Mac must run the **same** kvz version; compare the `kvz version` output
across the fleet. Homebrew installs the binary and the small Linux kernel that
pods boot; nothing else is needed. (Without Homebrew, unpack the release tarball
from the [releases page](https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/releases) and use
its `bin/kvz`; it finds the kernel in `share/kvz/kernel` next to it.)

Install `tart` too (`brew install cirruslabs/cli/tart`) only if you plan to run
macOS VM pods from OCI images.

## 5. Start the first server

On the first server Mac:

```sh
kvz install server                  # one server
# or, for high availability:
kvz install server --cluster-init
```

Add `--node-ip <address>` if the Mac has more than one possible address, and
`--tls-san <name>` for any extra DNS name you'll use to reach the API server.
`kvz install` writes a launchd service
(`~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.kvz.server.plist`) that starts now, at every login,
and again if kvz exits. Its log is `~/.kvz/logs/kvz-server.log`.

Wait until the node is Ready (usually a few seconds):

```sh
until kvz kubectl get nodes 2>/dev/null | grep -q ' Ready'; do sleep 1; done
kvz kubectl get nodes -o wide
```

Then collect the two things every other Mac needs:

```sh
cat ~/.kvz/join-token                                    # TOKEN, looks like K10…::…
awk '/server:/{print $2}' ~/.kvz/kubeconfig-external.yaml   # SERVER_URL, https://<address>:6443
```

`SERVER_URL` uses the address this server advertises. Check it's one the other
Macs can reach; if not, reinstall the server with `--node-ip`. Treat the token
like a password: it lets a machine join the cluster.

## 6. Add more servers (high availability only)

Skip this with a single server. On each additional server Mac, **one at a
time**:

```sh
kvz install server --server SERVER_URL --token TOKEN
```

Wait for it to be Ready before adding the next. Check from the first server:

```sh
kvz kubectl get nodes
```

New servers join etcd as learners and are promoted once they have caught up. HA
mode is remembered in each server's data directory, so the service needs no
extra flags after a restart.

## 7. Join the other Macs as agents

On every agent Mac (these can join in parallel):

```sh
kvz install agent --server SERVER_URL --token TOKEN
```

With several servers, any server's URL works: agents learn about every server
and keep a local load balancer in front of them, so they carry on when one goes
down. The agent's log is `~/.kvz/logs/kvz-agent.log`.

## 8. Verify the cluster

Run these on a server Mac (`kvz kubectl` uses `~/.kvz/kubeconfig.yaml` there).

**Every Mac is a Ready node, on the same version:**

```sh
kvz kubectl get nodes -o wide
```

**Pods start on every Mac, and reach each other across Macs:**

```sh
N=$(kvz kubectl get nodes --no-headers | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
kvz kubectl create deployment fleet-check --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=$((N*2))
kvz kubectl expose deployment fleet-check --port=80
kvz kubectl rollout status deployment/fleet-check --timeout=180s
kvz kubectl get pods -l app=fleet-check -o wide      # NODE column: every Mac should appear
for node in $(kvz kubectl get nodes -o name | cut -d/ -f2); do
  kvz kubectl run "net-$node" --rm -i --restart=Never --image=alpine:3.22 \
    --overrides="{\"spec\":{\"nodeName\":\"$node\"}}" -- \
    wget -qO- -T5 http://fleet-check.default.svc.cluster.local | grep -q 'Welcome to nginx' \
    && echo "$node: ok" || echo "$node: FAILED"
done
kvz kubectl delete deployment,service fleet-check
```

Every node must print `ok`. That one check covers pod start-up on each Mac,
cluster DNS, Services and the pod network between Macs.

## 9. Use the cluster from another computer

Each server writes `~/.kvz/kubeconfig-external.yaml`, which points at its own
address. Copy it to your laptop:

```sh
scp mini-01:.kvz/kubeconfig-external.yaml ~/.kube/kvz.yaml
KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/kvz.yaml kubectl get nodes
```

It holds cluster-admin credentials, so keep it private. The API server's
certificate covers the server's address and host name; add more names with
`--tls-san`.

## 10. Day-2 operations

| Task | How |
|---|---|
| Upgrade every Mac | Apply an `upgrade.cattle.io/v1` Plan; kvz drains and upgrades each Mac in turn, servers first, and rolls back a Mac whose new release doesn't start. See [upgrades.md](upgrades.md). This needs a release newer than v1.37.2-2; check with `kvz kubectl api-resources \| grep plans`. On older releases, `brew upgrade kvz` on each Mac, servers first. |
| Back up the datastore | `kvz etcd-snapshot save --name <name>` on a server; automatic snapshots run every 12 hours. See [operations.md](operations.md#backups-and-restores). |
| Add a Mac | Steps 2 to 4, then step 6 or 7. |
| Remove a Mac | `kvz kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data`, then on that Mac `kvz uninstall --purge`, then `kvz kubectl delete node <node>`. |
| Reboot a Mac | Just reboot. With automatic login, kvz comes back on its own. |
| Watch logs | `tail -f ~/.kvz/logs/kvz-server.log` (or `kvz-agent.log`) on that Mac. |
| Inspect a node's pod network | `kvz kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/debug/kvz/podnet` |
| Registry mirrors and credentials | `~/.kvz/registries.yaml` on every Mac. See [operations.md](operations.md#registry-mirrors). |

All flags and files are listed in [operations.md](operations.md).

## 11. Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `kvz install` fails with `launchctl bootstrap: … Bootstrap failed` | The user has no GUI login session | Turn on automatic login (step 2), reboot or log in once, run `kvz install` again |
| kvz stops after a reboot | The Mac is at the login window | Automatic login; FileVault must be off |
| An agent never appears in `get nodes` | It can't reach the server on 6443/6444, or the token is wrong | `nc -vz <server address> 6443` and `nc -vz <server address> 6444` from the agent; read `~/.kvz/logs/kvz-agent.log`; re-copy the token |
| `no route to host` to a LAN address that answers `ping` | macOS Local Network permission | Allow kvz under Privacy & Security → Local Network, or use Tailscale addresses |
| Two Macs show up as one node, or flip back and forth | Duplicate host names | Give each Mac a unique name (step 2) or `--node-name` |
| A node is `NotReady` | That Mac is asleep, offline or kvz isn't running | `pmset -g`, then `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/dev.kvz.agent` (or `dev.kvz.server`) and the log |
| `kubectl logs` / `exec` fail for pods on one Mac | Port 10250 on that Mac isn't reachable from the servers | Open it in the firewall or ACL |
| Pods on different Macs can't reach each other | Port 6446 is blocked, or `--node-ip` is an address the others can't reach | Open 6446; set `--node-ip` on that Mac and reinstall |
| Pods stay `Pending` on a full Mac | About 120 Linux pods per Mac is the limit (Virtualization.framework caps VMs per host) | Add Macs |
| Pods stuck in `ContainerCreating` | A volume, image or certificate isn't ready | `kvz kubectl describe pod <pod>`: the events say which |
| Everything else | | Run `kvz server --verbose` (or the agent) in a terminal after `kvz uninstall` to watch every component's logs live |

To change a service's flags, run `kvz install server|agent …` again with the
new flags; it replaces the old service.

## 12. Getting help and reporting problems

- **Source code and docs:** <https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz>
- **Bugs:** <https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/issues/new/choose>. Include
  `kvz version`, `sw_vers -productVersion`, the number of Macs and their roles,
  `kvz kubectl get nodes -o wide`, and the relevant part of
  `~/.kvz/logs/kvz-*.log`. **Remove join tokens and kubeconfig contents first.**
- **Questions and ideas:** <https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/discussions>
- **Security vulnerabilities:** report privately, never in a public issue:
  <https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/security/advisories/new> (see
  [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md)).
- **Releases and changelog:** <https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/releases>

# Getting started

This guide takes you from installing kvz to a cluster running all three kinds
of pods. It takes a few minutes.

## What you need

- An **Apple Silicon Mac** (M1 or later) running **macOS 26 or later**.
- **`kubectl`**, or use the one built into kvz (`kvz kubectl`).
- **`tart`**, only if you want macOS pods from OCI images.

## 1. Install kvz

```sh
brew install kvz-platform/tap/kvz
```

This installs `kvz` and the small Linux kernel that pods boot (about 9 MB).
Update later with `brew upgrade kvz`.

Without Homebrew, download `kvz-<version>-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` from the
[releases page](https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/releases), unpack it and run
`bin/kvz` from inside it (it finds the kernel in `share/kvz/kernel` next to it):

```sh
tar -xzf kvz-v1.37.2-2-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
cd kvz-v1.37.2-2-darwin-arm64
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine .   # only if a browser downloaded it
./bin/kvz server
```

Early releases are ad-hoc signed rather than notarized, so a browser download
needs the `xattr` line before macOS will run it. Homebrew and `curl` downloads
don't.

## 2. Or build from source

Skip this if you used Homebrew. To build from source you also need Go, the
Xcode command line tools, and Apple's `container` tool (used once, to build the
kernel).

```sh
git clone https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz && cd kvz
make build                 # bin/kvz, signed for Virtualization.framework
./kernel/build.sh          # the pod kernel, into ~/.kvz/kernel/Image
```

The steps below write `kvz`. From a source build, that's `./bin/kvz`.

## 3. Start the cluster

```sh
kvz server
```

kvz starts etcd, the API server, the scheduler, the controllers and a local
node, all in this one process. When it's ready it prints:

```
kvz server ready in 1.7s
  export KUBECONFIG=/Users/you/.kvz/kubeconfig.yaml
  join: kvz agent --server https://192.168.1.20:6443 --token <token in /Users/you/.kvz/join-token>
  logs: /Users/you/.kvz/kvz.log (--verbose to stream them here)
```

Copy the `export` line into another terminal. The `join` line is for adding
more Macs later. It doesn't show the join token itself, so the output is safe
to share; the token is in the file it names. The Kubernetes components log to
`kvz.log` rather than the terminal; run `kvz server --verbose` to see them
live. (When kvz runs as a service, or its output goes to a file or pipe, the
full logs go to that output as usual.)

## 4. Run a Linux pod

```sh
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kvz/kubeconfig.yaml
kubectl run web --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl get pods -o wide
```

The pod gets its own cold-booted VM and its own IP address. Pods without a
`runtimeClassName` use the Linux runtime.

## 5. Run a native macOS pod

Native pods are plain macOS processes. They're useful for anything that needs
the host itself, such as Xcode, code signing or the GPU.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hello-mac
spec:
  runtimeClassName: darwin
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: main
      image: host          # not pulled; native pods run on the host
      command: ["/usr/bin/sw_vers"]
```

```sh
kubectl apply -f hello-mac.yaml
kubectl logs hello-mac
```

Native pods must set `command`. Each pod gets its own working directory, passed
in as `$KVZ_POD_DIR`.

## 6. Run a macOS VM pod

A macOS pod is a full macOS virtual machine. Its disk is a copy-on-write clone,
so starting one is instant on disk, and the VM is ready for `exec` once SSH
answers (about 15 to 20 seconds).

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: mac
spec:
  runtimeClassName: macos
  containers:
    - name: vm
      image: ghcr.io/cirruslabs/macos-tahoe-base:latest
```

```sh
kubectl apply -f mac.yaml
kubectl exec mac -- sw_vers
```

macOS allows two macOS VMs per Mac. Extra macOS pods wait with the reason
`WaitingForVMSlot` until a slot frees up.

## 7. Add more Macs

On each extra Mac, install kvz and run the `join` command the server printed,
with the token from the server's `~/.kvz/join-token`:

```sh
kvz agent --server https://192.168.1.20:6443 --token K10…::…
```

The new Mac shows up in `kubectl get nodes`, and pods spread across all of
them. Pods on different Macs can reach each other and use the same Services.

For more than a couple of Macs (headless Mac minis, high availability, ports,
automatic login, verification), follow [Fleet setup](fleet.md).

## 8. Run kvz in the background

To keep kvz running after you close the terminal, and start it at login:

```sh
kvz install server        # or: kvz install agent --server … --token …
```

This installs a launchd service and starts it. Logs go to `~/.kvz/logs`. Remove
it with `kvz uninstall`.

## Next

- [Runtimes](runtimes.md): what each kind of pod is and how to pick one
- [Kubernetes features](kubernetes-features.md): what works today
- [Operations](operations.md): flags, snapshots and uninstalling

<!-- source: https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/blob/main/docs/operations.md -->

# Operations

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `kvz server` | Runs the control plane and, unless `--disable-agent` is set, a local node |
| `kvz agent --server URL --token TOKEN` | Joins this Mac to a cluster as a node |
| `kvz install server` / `kvz install agent …` | Installs kvz as a launchd service that starts now and at login |
| `kvz uninstall` | Removes the service. Add `--purge` to also delete `~/.kvz` |
| `kvz etcd-snapshot save` / `ls` / `delete` | Manages snapshots of the cluster datastore |
| `kvz kubectl …` | Runs a kubectl that matches the cluster's version |
| `kvz version` | Prints the version |

## Server flags

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--https-listen-port` | `6443` | API server port. The join endpoint uses the next port. |
| `--etcd-port` | `2379` | Embedded etcd client port |
| `--disable-agent` | off | Run only the control plane, with no local node |
| `--disable` | none | Skip bundled add-ons: `traefik`, `helm-controller`, `local-storage`, `metrics-server`, `upgrade-controller` |
| `--etcd-sync` | `barrier` | How etcd flushes writes: `full`, `barrier` (crash-consistent) or `none` |
| `--etcd-snapshot-interval` | `12h` | How often to take automatic snapshots. `0` turns them off. |
| `--etcd-snapshot-retention` | `5` | How many automatic snapshots to keep |
| `--cluster-reset-restore-path` | none | Restore the datastore from a snapshot before starting |
| `--cluster-init` | off | Start a cluster that more servers can join (high availability) |
| `--server`, `--token` | none | Join an existing cluster as another server |
| `--secrets-encryption` | off | Encrypt Secrets at rest (AES-CBC). Stays on once enabled. |
| `--kube-apiserver-arg`, `--kube-controller-manager-arg`, `--kube-scheduler-arg` | none | Extra flags for a component, as `name=value`; repeatable |
| `--tls-san` | none | Extra names or IPs for the API server certificate |

## Node flags (server and agent)

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--node-name` | the Mac's host name | Name of this node |
| `--node-ip` | the Tailscale IP if present, otherwise the main IP | Address other nodes use to reach this one |
| `--data-dir` | `~/.kvz` | Where kvz keeps its state |
| `--default-runtime` | `linux` | Runtime for pods without `runtimeClassName` |
| `--max-pods` | `1000` | Pod capacity of this node |
| `--kubelet-port` | `10250` | Port for `logs`, `exec` and metrics |
| `--overlay-port` | `6446` | Port of the pod network link between nodes |
| `--verbose` | off | Stream component logs to the terminal instead of `kvz.log` |

## Files

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `~/.kvz/kubeconfig.yaml` | Admin kubeconfig for the cluster |
| `~/.kvz/kernel/Image` | The pod kernel built by `kernel/build.sh`, used by source builds. Homebrew and release-tarball installs use the kernel shipped next to the binary (`$(brew --prefix)/share/kvz/kernel/Image`, plus its `config`) instead. Set `KVZ_KERNEL` to use another. |
| `~/.kvz/server/manifests/` | YAML here is applied automatically, like k3s |
| `~/.kvz/registries.yaml` | Registry mirrors and credentials (`KVZ_REGISTRIES` overrides the path) |
| `~/.kvz/server/db/snapshots/` | etcd snapshots |
| `~/.kvz/kvz.log` | Component logs when kvz runs in a terminal (the previous run's log is `kvz.log.1`) |
| `~/.kvz/join-token` | The token other Macs join with (`kvz agent --token`) |
| `~/.kvz/logs/` | Logs from the launchd service |
| `~/.kvz/upgrade/state.json` | An automated upgrade that hasn't been confirmed yet, or the release that was rolled back |
| `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.kvz.server.plist` | The installed service (or `dev.kvz.agent.plist`) |

## Backups and restores

```sh
kvz etcd-snapshot save --name before-upgrade
kvz etcd-snapshot ls
kvz server --cluster-reset-restore-path ~/.kvz/server/db/snapshots/<file>
```

The server also takes a snapshot every 12 hours and keeps the five newest.

## High availability

Start the first server with `--cluster-init`, then join more servers with the
same token. Each server runs the API server, controller-manager, scheduler
and an etcd member; three servers tolerate the loss of one.

```sh
kvz server --cluster-init                                       # first Mac
kvz server --server https://<first-mac>:6443 --token <token>    # each other server
kvz agent  --server https://<any-server>:6443 --token <token>   # worker Macs
```

New servers join etcd as learners and are promoted once they have caught up.
Agents keep a local load balancer in front of every server they know about, so
they keep working when one server goes down. HA mode is remembered in the data
dir, so restarts need no extra flags.

## Registry mirrors

`~/.kvz/registries.yaml` uses the k3s format. Mirrors are tried in order, then
the registry itself:

```yaml
mirrors:
  docker.io:
    endpoint: ["https://mirror.gcr.io"]
configs:
  registry.example.com:
    auth: {username: me, password: secret}
    tls: {ca_file: /path/to/ca.pem}
```

## Helm charts

The bundled Helm controller installs `HelmChart` objects, as in k3s:

```yaml
apiVersion: helm.cattle.io/v1
kind: HelmChart
metadata: {name: podinfo, namespace: kube-system}
spec:
  repo: https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo
  chart: podinfo
  targetNamespace: default
```

## Debugging a node

Every node serves Go profiles and a dump of its pod network (switch ports,
addresses and the gateway's ARP cache) through the API server:

```sh
kvz kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/debug/kvz/podnet
kvz kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2"
```

## Upgrades

To upgrade a whole cluster, apply an `upgrade.cattle.io/v1` Plan, the same API
as the k3s system-upgrade-controller. kvz cordons, drains and upgrades each Mac
in turn, control plane first, and rolls a node back if the new release doesn't
start. See [upgrades.md](upgrades.md).

Upgrading kvz upgrades the embedded etcd too, and etcd can't move a data
directory back to an older version. Take a snapshot before upgrading
(`kvz etcd-snapshot save`) if you might roll back.

With several Macs, upgrade the servers first, then the agents, and don't leave
them on different kvz versions longer than you need to (mixed versions aren't
tested). Going from kvz on Kubernetes 1.35 straight to 1.37
was tested on a running two-node cluster; existing objects and nodes carried
over.

## Joining Macs securely

The join token looks like `K10<hash>::<secret>`, the same format as k3s. The
hash pins the cluster's certificate authority, so a new node can verify the
server before it sends the secret. Each node then gets its own certificate,
limited to what a node is allowed to do.

## Uninstalling

```sh
kvz uninstall            # remove the launchd service
kvz uninstall --purge    # also delete ~/.kvz: cluster state, images, kernel and volumes
```

---

<!-- source: https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/blob/main/docs/upgrades.md -->

# Automated upgrades

kvz upgrades itself across a cluster from `upgrade.cattle.io/v1` **Plan**
objects, the same API as the k3s
[system-upgrade-controller](https://docs.k3s.io/upgrades/automated). Plans
written for k3s apply unchanged; kvz runs the controller itself, so there is
nothing to install.

```yaml
apiVersion: upgrade.cattle.io/v1
kind: Plan
metadata:
  name: kvz
  namespace: system-upgrade
spec:
  concurrency: 1
  cordon: true
  drain: {force: true, timeout: 5m}
  version: v1.35.10-2          # or: channel: https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/releases/latest
```

```sh
kvz kubectl create namespace system-upgrade
kvz kubectl apply -f plan.yaml
kvz kubectl -n system-upgrade get plans -o wide
```

## What happens

1. The server resolves the Plan's `version`. A `channel` resolves to the last
   path element of the URL it redirects to, so GitHub's `releases/latest`
   works. Channels are checked every 15 minutes.
2. It picks the nodes matching `nodeSelector` (all nodes if unset).
   Control-plane nodes go first, as with k3s: workers don't start until every
   control-plane node in the Plan is done. Then up to `concurrency` nodes
   (default 1) run at a time.
3. With `cordon` or `drain`, it cordons the node, and with `drain` evicts its
   pods (`kubectl drain` semantics: `force`, `timeout`, `gracePeriod`,
   `deleteEmptydirData`, `ignoreDaemonSets` (default true), `disableEviction`,
   `podSelector`).
4. The node's kvz downloads
   `kvz-<version>-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` and checks it against its `.sha256`.
   It then checks the new binary itself: a valid code signature, the
   virtualization entitlement, the same signing team as the running binary
   (when that one is Developer ID signed), and that `kvz version` reports the
   expected release.
5. It swaps `bin/kvz` and, for Homebrew and tarball installs, the pod kernel
   in `share/kvz/kernel`. Each rename is atomic, and the old files are kept as
   `*.prev`. Then kvz restarts.
6. When the node is Ready on the new release, the server uncordons it (unless
   it was cordoned before), labels it `plan.upgrade.cattle.io/<plan>=<hash>`
   and moves on.

A node already on the Plan's version is just labeled. Upgrading the server
restarts the API server; the controller picks up where it left off, because
its progress is kept on the Node objects.

## Restarts and rollback

Run kvz as a service (`kvz install server|agent`). Under launchd, kvz exits
after installing the new binary and launchd starts it again. That also makes
rollback possible: a newly installed binary that starts three times without its
node becoming Ready puts the previous files back and restarts into them. The
node then reports
`Failed: <version> started 3 times without its node becoming Ready; rolled
back to <previous>`, and the Plan stays incomplete until you change its
version.

In a terminal, kvz starts the new binary itself and exits, so the new kvz runs
in the background. There is nothing to restart a binary that keeps crashing,
so there is no automatic rollback in that mode.

## Status

```sh
kvz kubectl -n system-upgrade get plans -o wide           # Complete and a per-node message
kvz kubectl get nodes -L plan.upgrade.cattle.io/kvz
kvz kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}'
```

| Annotation on the node | Set by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `kvz.dev/release` | node | The kvz release the node runs (set once it's Ready on it) |
| `upgrade.kvz.dev/plan` | server | The Plan upgrading this node |
| `upgrade.kvz.dev/apply`, `upgrade.kvz.dev/url` | server | Install this release from this URL (set after the drain) |
| `upgrade.kvz.dev/status` | node | `Downloading`, `Verifying`, `Restarting into …`, `Failed: …` |

A failed download or check is retried every 2 minutes and leaves the node
cordoned, as upstream does. Deleting a Plan releases its nodes and uncordons
the ones it had cordoned.

## kvz-specific settings

| Plan annotation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `upgrade.kvz.dev/release-url` | Tarball URL template, e.g. `https://mirror.example.com/kvz-{version}-darwin-arm64.tar.gz`. The checksum must be at the same URL plus `.sha256`. |
| `upgrade.kvz.dev/allow-downgrade: "true"` | Allow moving to a lower release number. Downgrades are refused by default, because etcd can't open a data directory written by a newer version. Take a snapshot first. |

Fields that only make sense for upstream's Job-based upgrades (`upgrade.image`,
`prepare`, `serviceAccountName`, `tolerations`, `secrets`) are accepted and
ignored.

## Notes

- Nodes running a kvz without this feature can't upgrade themselves. Upgrade
  them once by hand (`brew upgrade kvz`, or the release tarball).
- A server started with `--disable-agent` has no node, so Plans can't select
  it. Upgrade it by hand.
- Homebrew installs are upgraded in place inside the Cellar. Homebrew still
  lists the old version until the next `brew upgrade kvz`, which installs the
  same files.
- If you run the upstream system-upgrade-controller instead, start servers
  with `--disable upgrade-controller`.

---

<!-- source: https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/blob/main/docs/runtimes.md -->

# Runtimes

Every kvz node runs pods in one of four runtimes. You pick one with the pod's
`runtimeClassName`. kvz creates the matching RuntimeClass objects for you when
the server starts.

| `runtimeClassName` | A pod is | Ready in | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `linux` (default) | its own Linux microVM | about 100 ms | ordinary container images |
| `macos` | a full macOS virtual machine | 15 to 20 s | macOS CI, testing on a clean macOS |
| `darwin` | native macOS processes on the host | about 15 to 50 ms | Xcode, code signing, GPU work |
| `apple` | a container run by Apple's `container` tool | about 0.6 to 0.8 s | the original v1 runtime, kept for comparison |

## linux

This is the default, so pods without a `runtimeClassName` land here.

Each pod boots its own small VM through Apple's Virtualization.framework:

- **Kernel and init:** the kvz kernel (8.5 MB) and a tiny init program that
  starts your container.
- **Filesystem:** the image is shared into the VM read-only, with a writable
  layer on top in memory.
- **Network:** each pod gets its own IP address on kvz's pod network.

Nothing is pre-started or cached: every pod is a cold boot, and it still
reaches Ready in about 100 ms.

**Limits.**

- **VMs per Mac:** Virtualization.framework allows about 127 VMs per Mac. kvz
  runs up to 120 pod VMs per node and queues the rest with the reason
  `WaitingForVMSlot`. Add more Macs to go past that.
- **Pod-to-pod bandwidth:** because pods don't share a kernel, traffic between
  them is slower than in a single-VM cluster. It measures 30 to 50 Gbps per
  stream, against about 85 Gbps elsewhere.

## macos

A macOS pod is a whole macOS virtual machine. The image can be:

- a local VM bundle in tart's layout (`disk.img`, `nvram.bin`, `config.json`),
- a path to such a bundle, or
- an OCI image reference, which kvz pulls with `tart pull`.

When the pod starts, kvz clones the disk with APFS `clonefile`. That's instant
even for a 50 GB disk, and the clone is thrown away when the pod is deleted. The
pod becomes Ready once the guest answers SSH. `kubectl exec` and `kubectl logs`
run over that SSH connection.

If the first container sets a `command`, kvz runs it inside the guest. Its exit
code ends the pod, which makes macOS pods work well as Jobs.

**Limits.** macOS allows two macOS VMs per Mac. Extra macOS pods wait with
`WaitingForVMSlot`.

## darwin

A native pod runs its containers as ordinary processes on the Mac itself, with:

- **A working directory:** each pod gets its own, passed in as `$KVZ_POD_DIR`.
- **Restarts:** handled with the pod's `restartPolicy`, backing off like the
  kubelet does.
- **Clean shutdown:** deleting the pod stops its whole process group, honoring
  the grace period.

Native pods must set `command`. The `image` field is required by Kubernetes, but
this runtime doesn't use it.

Native pods share the host's network, so they use the Mac's own IP address.

## apple

This was kvz's first Linux runtime. It runs each container through Apple's
`container` daemon. That daemon starts VMs one at a time, at about two per
second, so it's much slower under load than `linux`. It's kept mainly as a
benchmark baseline.

## Choosing a default

The node flag `--default-runtime` sets the runtime for pods without a
`runtimeClassName`. It defaults to `linux`.

---

<!-- source: https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/blob/main/docs/kubernetes-features.md -->

# Kubernetes features

kvz runs upstream Kubernetes 1.37 (kube-apiserver, controller-manager and
scheduler, unmodified) with embedded etcd 3.7. It is tested with the full
Sonobuoy certified-conformance suite on a two-node cluster; see
[Conformance](#conformance). This page lists what works today and the known
limits.

## Workloads

- Deployments (scaling, rollouts), StatefulSets (with stable pod DNS names),
  Jobs and plain Pods
- Init containers, native sidecars, and `restartPolicy` with real
  `CrashLoopBackOff` back-off
- Startup, readiness and liveness probes (exec, HTTP, TCP; gRPC is checked as
  TCP), `readinessGates`
- `postStart` and `preStop` hooks, termination messages (including
  `FallbackToLogsOnError`), `activeDeadlineSeconds`
- Ephemeral containers (`kubectl debug`), which run inside the pod's VM and
  share its network and processes
- Kubelet-style pod events and condition reasons, `observedGeneration`

## Resources and security

- **CPU and memory limits** are enforced per container with cgroup v2
  (`cpu.max`, `cpu.weight`, `memory.max`), exactly as on a Linux node. A
  container that exceeds its memory limit is reported as `OOMKilled`.
- **In-place resize** (`kubectl patch --subresource resize`) updates the limits
  of running containers, or restarts them where `resizePolicy` asks for it.
- Pods without a CPU limit can use every core of the Mac; pods without a
  memory limit get 2 GiB (`KVZ_DEFAULT_MEMORY_MB`). Guest memory is only
  backed by the Mac when it is used.
- **Security context:** `runAsUser`, `runAsGroup`, `supplementalGroups`,
  `fsGroup`, `runAsNonRoot`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `privileged`,
  capabilities (containerd's default set, plus `add` and `drop`) and
  `allowPrivilegeEscalation`.
- **Sysctls:** every pod has its own kernel, so all sysctls are pod-scoped
  and allowed.
- Each pod is its own VM: containers in different pods never share a kernel.

## kubectl

`exec` (with a terminal), `logs` (including `-f`, `--previous`, `--since` and
`--tail`), `port-forward`, `attach` (interactive for containers with
`stdin`/`tty`), `debug`, `cp`, `run --rm -i` and `top`.
kvz also bundles a version-matched kubectl as
`kvz kubectl`.

## Networking

- **Pod network:** every Linux pod has its own IP address on kvz's pod network,
  an in-process switch. Pods on different Macs reach each other over an
  authenticated overlay between nodes.
- **Services:** `ClusterIP` load balancing across replicas, plus `NodePort` and
  `LoadBalancer`, which are exposed on the Mac. `sessionAffinity: ClientIP`
  works for all three.
- **Cluster DNS:** a built-in server at `10.43.0.10` that answers
  `cluster.local` like CoreDNS: service and headless records, StatefulSet pod
  names, SRV, ExternalName, pod (`a-b-c-d.<ns>.pod`) and reverse records.
  Other names go to the Mac's resolvers, so VPN and Tailscale names resolve
  too. `dnsPolicy` and `dnsConfig` work.
- **The API server reaches pods** (on every node), so admission and conversion
  webhooks, aggregated API servers running in pods, and `kubectl proxy` to
  pods and services work.
- **NetworkPolicy:** enforced in the pod switch, for ingress and egress, pod and
  namespace selectors, IP blocks and ports.
- **Ingress:** Traefik is installed by default.
- **Host networking:** `hostPort` (TCP and UDP, `hostIP`, conflict checks) and
  `hostNetwork`. A `hostNetwork` pod shares the Mac's network as on a Linux
  node: `127.0.0.1` and the node IP inside it are the Mac's, and every socket it
  listens on appears on the Mac at the same address and port.

## Storage and configuration

- ConfigMaps and Secrets, including live updates to mounted volumes (within
  about a second), `defaultMode` and item modes, optional sources
- `emptyDir` (including `medium: Memory`), `hostPath` (directories and files),
  projected and downward API volumes, `subPath` and `subPathExpr`
- PersistentVolumeClaims through the built-in local-path provisioner, which is
  the default StorageClass
- Service account tokens bound to the pod, so in-cluster clients work
- Image volumes (`volumes[].image`): an OCI image's files mounted read-only,
  straight from the image store with nothing copied
- `clusterTrustBundle` projections (CA bundles by name, or by signer and
  label selector) and `podCertificate` projections (a per-pod key and
  certificate from a signer, refreshed before expiry), using the kubelet's own
  managers. Their files keep the volume's default mode: kvz can't yet set the
  per-file owner (`user`, `fsGroup`) that makes the kubelet use 0600.

## Images

- Pull policies `Always`, `IfNotPresent` and `Never`
- `imagePullSecrets` and Docker config credentials
- `ErrImagePull` and `ImagePullBackOff` with retries
- One shared store, keyed by image digest
- Registry mirrors and credentials in `~/.kvz/registries.yaml`, in the k3s
  format (see [Operations](operations.md#registry-mirrors))

## Metrics

kvz reports per-container CPU and memory from inside each pod VM and serves the
`metrics.k8s.io` API, so `kubectl top` and HorizontalPodAutoscalers work. Each
node also serves the kubelet's `/metrics`, `/metrics/cadvisor` and
`/metrics/resource`, so Prometheus and an upstream metrics-server can scrape
it.

## Add-ons installed by default

Traefik, the local-path provisioner, the metrics server and the k3s Helm
controller (so `HelmChart` objects install charts). Skip any of them with
`--disable traefik`, `--disable local-storage`, `--disable metrics-server` or
`--disable helm-controller`. Put your own manifests in
`~/.kvz/server/manifests` and kvz applies them automatically.

## Known limits

| Limit | Why |
|---|---|
| About 120 Linux pods per Mac | Virtualization.framework caps a Mac at about 127 VMs. Add Macs to scale out. |
| Two macOS pods per Mac | macOS itself allows only two macOS guests per host |
| Pod-to-pod bandwidth around 30 to 50 Gbps | Each pod is its own VM, so traffic can't stay inside one kernel |
| Large bursts are CPU-bound | Starting a VM costs about 65 ms of CPU in Virtualization.framework |
| No user namespaces, AppArmor or seccomp profiles | The VM boundary isolates pods; inside a pod, containers rely on capabilities |

## Conformance

kvz passes the full Kubernetes conformance suite:
`sonobuoy run --mode certified-conformance` on a two-node cluster (two kvz nodes
on an M5 Max) reports **454 of 454 tests passed** (Kubernetes 1.37.2).

---

<!-- source: https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md -->

# kvz architecture

kvz is a k3s-shaped Kubernetes distribution for Apple Silicon Macs. One signed
darwin/arm64 binary runs the whole control plane in-process, natively on
macOS, plus a node agent whose pods are native macOS workloads.

```
                    ┌──────────────────────────── kvz server (one darwin process) ────────────────────────────┐
 kubectl ──TLS──▶   │ kube-apiserver ── etcd (embedded, F_BARRIERFSYNC WAL) │ controller-manager │ scheduler   │
                    │       ▲                                                                                  │
                    │       │ client-go (node identity)                                                        │
                    │  kvz node (virtual-kubelet, tuned queues) ── Provider mux (by RuntimeClass) ─┐            │
                    │                                                                               │            │
                    │  podnet: L2 switch + gateway + DHCP/DNS (gVisor netstack), 10.88.0.0/16 ◀───┼──┐         │
                    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──┼─────────┘
                ┌────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬────────────────────┘  │ SOCK_DGRAM socketpair
                ▼                            ▼                          ▼                       │ per VM NIC
   linux (default)                 macos                        darwin                         │
   kvz microVM per pod             macOS VM per pod             native processes               │
   kvz kernel + kvz-init (PID 1)   APFS clone, DHCP on podnet   fork/exec, pgid kill           │
   virtiofs image + tmpfs overlay  SSH exec over podnet                                        │
   vsock events + exec ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   apple: Apple `container` daemon (v1 runtime, kept for comparison)
```

## Control plane

* `k8s.io/kubernetes` v1.37.2 is imported as a library (staging modules pinned,
  no fork). kube-apiserver, controller-manager and scheduler run in one darwin
  process. Two shims make that possible:
  * `logsapi.ReapplyHandling = ReapplyHandlingIgnoreUnchanged`
  * scheduler via `app.Setup`/`app.Run`, avoiding a second process-wide signal
    handler
* **etcd WAL sync.** On darwin, etcd fsyncs with `F_FULLFSYNC`, which flushes
  the SSD cache on every commit (≈4 ms per write). kvz vendors etcd's `fileutil`
  and defaults to `F_BARRIERFSYNC`. It's a write-ordering barrier: crash-
  consistent, though the most recent commits can be lost on sudden power loss.
  It's what Apple recommends for databases, and roughly what a Linux guest's
  fsync gets on Virtualization.framework anyway. `--etcd-sync=full` restores
  strict durability. Effect: create→watch 4.0 → 0.5 ms.
* **Local kubeconfig uses loopback.** Talking to the host's own Tailscale
  address went through the VPN's network extension and cut API throughput
  about 3×. `kubeconfig-external.yaml` carries the routable address.
* Scheduler API QPS is raised to 500/1000. Cloud and volume controllers that
  don't apply are disabled.
* PKI: one ECDSA CA, Node+RBAC authorization, and k3s-style join tokens
  (`K10<ca-sha256>::<secret>`).

## Node (virtual-kubelet, vendored)

* The pod controller is built directly, with a 2000 qps work-queue limiter
  instead of client-go's default 10 qps (50 native pods: 6.8 s → 0.42 s).
* **Patch:** finalize deleted pods as soon as the provider has stopped them.
  Upstream always slept `DeletionGracePeriodSeconds` (1 pod: 1.05 s → 54 ms).
* The provider pushes status through `PodNotifier`; there's no polling.

## linux runtime: kvz microVMs

Every pod is a cold-booted Linux microVM, built from scratch to boot fast:

| piece | what it does | why |
|---|---|---|
| **kvz microVM monitor** (`pkg/microvm`) | Virtualization.framework through Code-Hex/vz, one VM per pod, booted concurrently | Apple's `container` daemon serializes VM starts at ~2/s per host |
| **kvz kernel** (`kernel/`) | Linux 6.18 LTS from `allnoconfig` plus only what pods need, everything built in, 8.5 MB | Apple's 30 MB debug kernel takes 106 ms to reach init; this one takes 17 ms |
| **kvz-init** (`cmd/kvz-init`, Go, static) | PID 1 from an uncompressed initramfs. Mounts proc/dev, the virtiofs share and the overlay root; configures the NIC over netlink; forks/chroots/execs the containers; reaps; restart policy; exec server | No init system, no image-format decoding, no DHCP; it reads `spec.json` and execs |
| **rootfs** | Image unpacked once into the image store; every pod VM mounts it read-only over virtiofs, with a tmpfs upper dir in the guest (overlayfs) | Zero per-pod host disk work, and pods share the host page cache |
| **one virtiofs device** | Multi-directory share: pod dir, image(s), hostPath volumes | Each virtio-pci device costs ~7 ms of guest boot |
| **events over vsock** | `init` / `hello` / `started` / `exit` pushed to the host | Status goes straight to the API |
| **exec over vsock** | Framed stdin/stdout/stderr/resize/exit protocol; pty support | `kubectl exec` without sshd in the guest |
| **IP on spec** | The host allocates the pod IP before boot; the guest sets it over netlink without waiting for carrier | Kernel IP autoconfig waited ~25 ms for link carrier |

Containers of a pod share the VM, so they share the pod's network namespace
and IP, as in Kubernetes. Restart policy is implemented in kvz-init with
kubelet-style `CrashLoopBackOff` status.

### Cold boot timeline (single pod, Studio)

```
 0 ms   CreatePod → spec.json written, NIC socketpair created
 1 ms   VZVirtualMachine created
65 ms   VZ start returns (VZ XPC process up, memory mapped, kernel loaded)
82 ms   kernel → /init (17 ms guest time)
84 ms   overlay mounted, NIC configured, container exec'd → "started"
~105–140 ms   pod Ready observed by a watching client (via apiserver)
```

## Pod network (`pkg/podnet`)

Each node runs an in-process L2 switch plus L3 gateway (gVisor netstack via
gvisor-tap-vsock). A pod VM's NIC is one end of a `SOCK_DGRAM` socketpair
handed to `VZFileHandleNetworkDeviceAttachment`.

* **Why not VZ NAT:** every NAT-attached VM creates a kernel `vmenet`
  interface. Hard-stopped VMs leaked them on the Studio until the host
  refused to create more (~251). From then on no VZ guest on that machine,
  kvz's or anyone else's, had networking until reboot. With podnet a NIC is
  just an fd.
* Pod-to-pod traffic is switched in-process. Egress is NATed through host
  sockets by the netstack, and DNS is served by the gateway.
* `kubectl port-forward` dials the pod through the netstack.
* macOS guests use the same network and get DHCP from the in-process server.
* Static pod IPs come from the top half of the CIDR, DHCP from the bottom.

## Bugs found and fixed upstream-style (vendored under `third_party/`)

* **Code-Hex/vz:** vsock connections double-closed the fd owned by
  `VZVirtioSocketConnection`. Under concurrency the second close hit whatever
  file had reused the number (random EBADF, VMs failing to start). Fixed with
  dup.
* **Code-Hex/vz:** `NewFileHandleNetworkDeviceAttachment` keeps no reference
  to the `*os.File`, so Go's finalizer could close a live NIC. kvz owns the
  file for the VM's lifetime.
* **virtual-kubelet:** the grace-period sleep before finalizing deletion
  (above).

## macos runtime
APFS `clonefile` of the VM bundle (a 50 GB disk in under 1 ms), a fresh
machine identifier, a NIC on podnet, DHCP from the in-process server, and
readiness gated on a working SSH login. If container 0 has a command, it runs
over SSH and its exit completes the pod. The kernel limit is 2 concurrent macOS
guests per host (`kvz.dev/macos-vm: 2`).

## darwin runtime
Native processes with a per-pod working dir, process-group kill honoring the
grace period, and restart policy with backoff.

## Limits
* **~127 concurrent VMs per Mac:** a hard Virtualization.framework /
  hypervisor limit, independent of guest RAM, and so a cap on concurrent
  linux pods per node. Native darwin pods aren't affected. Multi-Mac clusters
  scale it out.
* Not implemented yet: Services/kube-proxy, cluster DNS, cross-node pod
  routing, projected SA tokens in pod volumes, stats summary.

---

<!-- source: https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/blob/main/SECURITY.md -->

# Security policy

kvz runs a Kubernetes control plane and starts virtual machines on your Mac,
so we take security reports seriously.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Please don't open a public issue.** Report it privately through GitHub:

**[Report a vulnerability](https://github.com/kvz-platform/kvz/security/advisories/new)**

Include what you found, how to reproduce it, the kvz version (`kvz version`)
and your macOS version. If you have a fix in mind, describe it, but don't open
a public pull request for it.

## What to expect

- We aim to acknowledge your report within **3 business days**.
- We'll keep you updated while we investigate, and agree on a disclosure date
  with you. We aim to release a fix within **90 days**, sooner for severe issues.
- Once a fix is released, we publish a GitHub security advisory and credit you,
  unless you'd rather stay anonymous.

## Supported versions

Only the **latest release** gets security fixes. kvz releases are cumulative,
so upgrading (`brew upgrade kvz`) is how you pick up a fix.

## Scope

In scope: the `kvz` binary and everything it runs, including the control plane,
the node agent, the pod network, the join protocol and tokens, the guest init
inside pod VMs, and the release artifacts and Homebrew formula.

Out of scope: vulnerabilities in upstream Kubernetes, etcd or macOS itself.
Report those to their projects. If kvz makes one of them worse or easier to
reach, that part is in scope.
